title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging and Stimulation in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation: A Review

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Post-stroke motor impairment is best understood as a disorder of distributed motor networks rather than a purely focal lesion effect. Damage to primary motor cortex, corticospinal pathways, or connected premotor and subcortical nodes perturbs the excitability and coordination of interconnected cortical and subcortical circuits, producing deficits that extend beyond the anatomical infarct. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been especially valuable for probing these disturbances, because it provides causal measures of corticospinal output, intracortical inhibition, and interregional motor control in humans ref [2], ref [15].

A central concept in early recovery models is that stroke induces an imbalance between the lesioned and contralesional hemispheres, with abnormal inhibitory and facilitatory interactions shaping residual motor output. TMS studies and stimulation-based models of plasticity indicate that post-stroke recovery depends on dynamic reweighting of excitatory and inhibitory mechanisms, rather than simple restoration of pre-stroke organization ref [15], ref [35], ref [37]. This view aligns with evidence that noninvasive stimulation can induce lasting, plasticity-like changes in cortical networks, thereby offering an experimental framework for understanding spontaneous and therapy-induced motor reorganization ref [35], ref [37].

Neuroimaging further reinforces the network perspective by showing that focal stimulation influences widespread motor circuits, including cortical and subcortical regions remote from the stimulation site ref [25], ref [31]. Such findings are directly relevant to stroke, where diaschisis and compensatory recruitment emerge at the systems level. Although most mechanistic work has been performed outside stroke populations, clinical studies and meta-analytic evidence suggest that modulating these network interactions can improve motor outcomes after stroke, supporting the translational importance of distributed motor network models ref [39]. More broadly, combined stimulation-imaging studies in other post-stroke domains also illustrate how contralesional regions may be either adaptive or maladaptive depending on recovery stage and network context ref [42].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A useful framework for understanding post-stroke motor dysfunction is that focal injury perturbs a distributed and dynamically coupled motor network rather than only destroying a local cortical node. Evidence from concurrent stimulation-imaging studies shows that transcranial magnetic stimulation can induce intensity-dependent bilateral changes in BOLD activity, indicating that perturbation of one hemisphere propagates through interhemispheric and subcortical pathways rather than remaining spatially confined ref [14]. This systems-level view is central to stroke, where altered coupling between ipsilesional and contralesional motor areas can contribute to impaired movement and maladaptive compensation.

The concept of interhemispheric imbalance is further supported by work showing that noninvasive stimulation modifies both local neurochemistry and large-scale functional connectivity. In particular, transcranial direct current stimulation has been linked to changes in GABA-related inhibition together with altered resting-state network organization, suggesting a mechanistic bridge between cortical excitability and network-level reorganization ref [40]. Such findings are highly relevant to post-stroke recovery, in which excessive inhibition of the ipsilesional motor cortex or inefficient recruitment of homologous regions may limit restitution of more normal motor patterns.

Recovery therefore depends on neuroplastic processes that unfold across synaptic, neurochemical, and network scales. Experimental work on repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation demonstrates lasting effects on markers of plasticity, although these effects depend on brain state and experimental context, underscoring that stimulation-induced reorganization is biologically conditional rather than uniform ref [13]. More broadly, consensus work on transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial direct current stimulation emphasizes their capacity to modulate motor learning and memory formation, which aligns with the principle that rehabilitation gains arise from experience-dependent reweighting of surviving motor circuits ref [15]. In this context, accurate targeting becomes crucial, because the functional consequences of stimulation depend on which residual nodes within the reorganizing motor network are engaged; neuronavigated approaches are therefore especially important for interrogating and modulating post-stroke motor system recovery ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A useful conceptual bridge between post-stroke motor network dysfunction and later therapeutic intervention is provided by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), which can probe corticospinal excitability, intracortical inhibition, and interhemispheric interactions at high temporal resolution. In stroke, these measures help operationalize motor network imbalance, revealing how damage to one hemisphere alters excitability within ipsilesional motor cortex and changes transcallosal influences from the contralesional side ref [11], ref [39]. Thus, TMS is not only a stimulation tool but also a systems-level assay of residual motor pathway integrity and reorganization.

Mechanistically, the physiological interpretation of TMS-derived markers depends on how induced currents recruit cortical neurons and local circuits. Foundational work on the mechanisms of magnetic stimulation emphasizes that TMS effects are shaped by axonal orientation, membrane properties, and synaptic connectivity, while computational modeling further shows that pulse waveform, coil geometry, and cortical folding strongly influence which neuronal populations are activated ref [31], ref [24]. These principles are especially relevant after stroke, where lesion-induced changes in anatomy and conductivity may distort the relation between stimulation intensity and effective circuit engagement.

At the network level, combining TMS with functional imaging or electroencephalography has clarified that focal perturbation can evoke distributed responses across sensorimotor and associative regions rather than purely local effects. TMS-fMRI studies demonstrate the opportunity—and methodological constraints—of mapping causal interactions within large-scale networks, whereas TMS-EEG provides a direct window onto cortical reactivity and effective connectivity with millisecond precision ref [14], ref [35]. In the stroke context, such multimodal approaches are valuable for distinguishing adaptive from maladaptive reorganization and for identifying candidate targets and timing for individualized neuromodulation-based rehabilitation ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central principle of post-stroke motor recovery is that impairment reflects dysfunction of distributed corticospinal and cortico-cortical networks rather than only focal tissue loss. In this context, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has become a key physiological tool for probing corticospinal excitability, intracortical inhibition/facilitation, conduction integrity, and interhemispheric interactions, thereby linking clinical deficits to measurable network-level disturbances ref [22], ref [23], ref [42]. These measures are particularly informative for characterizing the imbalance that often emerges between the lesioned and contralesional hemispheres after stroke, which can constrain restitution of motor output.

Evidence from combined functional MRI and TMS studies further indicates that successful early recovery is accompanied by dynamic reorganization of motor representations rather than simple reinstatement of the premorbid pattern. Rapidly recovering patients can show evolving recruitment of ipsilesional and contralesional motor areas together with changes in TMS-derived motor maps and excitability, supporting the view that recovery depends on flexible reweighting within the motor network ref [19]. This systems-level perspective helps explain why recovery trajectories differ across patients with similar lesion locations but different residual connectivity and physiological reserve.

These concepts also motivate therapeutic neuromodulation. Repetitive TMS and related noninvasive brain stimulation approaches are used either to upregulate hypoexcitable ipsilesional motor regions or to downregulate excessive contralesional inhibition, with the aim of normalizing interhemispheric balance and promoting use-dependent plasticity ref [42], ref [23]. Although most work has focused on the upper limb, analogous principles are increasingly being extended to gait, balance, and lower-limb recovery, underscoring that post-stroke rehabilitation should be framed at the level of distributed motor networks rather than isolated cortical foci ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Post-Stroke Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
These network-level models of post-stroke dysfunction directly motivate noninvasive brain stimulation as a tool to probe and reshape maladaptive motor circuit dynamics. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) provides a causal method for assessing corticospinal excitability, interhemispheric interactions, and the functional integrity of residual motor pathways, thereby linking systems-level reorganization to measurable physiological targets ref [12], ref [30]. In this framework, recovery is not viewed solely as local tissue repair, but as progressive rebalancing of distributed motor network activity through plastic changes that may be spontaneous or therapy-induced ref [33], ref [34].

A central translational idea is that stroke can produce excessive inhibitory drive from the contralesional hemisphere onto ipsilesional motor areas, and that stimulation protocols may counter this imbalance in either direction. Consistent with this concept, excitatory and inhibitory repetitive TMS can induce bidirectional changes in interhemispheric resting-state functional connectivity, supporting the view that externally applied stimulation is capable of reorganizing large-scale coupling rather than only modifying focal excitability ref [11]. This systems perspective helps explain why both ipsilesional facilitation and contralesional suppression have been explored in motor rehabilitation after stroke ref [30], ref [33].

The rationale for image-guided stimulation further follows from the heterogeneity of lesion anatomy and post-stroke remapping. Neuronavigated TMS shows meaningful spatial congruence with functional neuroimaging, suggesting that individualized targeting can better align stimulation with surviving motor network nodes and potentially improve mechanistic specificity ref [36]. At the same time, cellular and molecular work indicates that repetitive magnetic stimulation engages synaptic plasticity-related processes beyond immediate electrophysiological effects, reinforcing its relevance to longer-term recovery and consolidation in rehabilitation paradigms ref [34], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a central noninvasive neurophysiological tool for probing corticospinal tract integrity and cortical excitability after stroke. Single-pulse paradigms quantify motor threshold, motor evoked potential presence and amplitude, central motor conduction time, and cortical map characteristics, thereby providing bedside indices of residual motor system function and recovery potential ref [1], ref [15]. Because these measures are frequently used to stratify impairment severity and monitor longitudinal change, rigorous attention to stimulation parameters, contraindications, and reporting standards is essential for both research and clinical translation ref [31], ref [1].

Methodological refinements are particularly important in lesioned brains, where anatomical variability can distort stimulation estimates. Neuronavigation improves spatial precision and reproducibility of motor hotspot localization, enabling more reliable mapping of spared motor representations and their reorganization over time ref [26]. Likewise, accounting for scalp-cortex distance can reduce bias in motor-threshold estimation, an issue especially relevant when stroke-related atrophy or lesion geometry alters effective field strength at the cortex ref [32]. These considerations make TMS not only a physiological assay, but also a more robust biomarker platform for interindividual comparisons.

Beyond stand-alone assessment, TMS gains interpretive value when integrated with neuroimaging. Consensus recommendations emphasize that combining stimulation with structural or functional imaging can link excitability measures to lesion location, network recruitment, and diaschisis, thereby clarifying why patients with similar clinical deficits may show different recovery trajectories ref [31]. Although repetitive TMS is primarily discussed as an intervention, meta-analytic evidence that stimulation-induced modulation can alter motor outcomes also underscores the relevance of TMS-derived excitability markers for identifying treatment-responsive phenotypes in stroke rehabilitation ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) provides a practical neurophysiological window into corticospinal system integrity after stroke, particularly through motor-evoked responses, motor threshold estimation, and mapping of residual cortical representations. For rehabilitation studies, however, the interpretability of these measures depends strongly on methodological rigor. An international consensus checklist has emphasized standardized reporting of stimulation intensity, hotspot definition, coil orientation, and participant state, all of which materially influence motor system readouts and their comparability across cohorts ref [22]. Test–retest work further shows that reliability varies across muscle representations, underscoring the need to select target muscles and acquisition procedures carefully when tracking longitudinal recovery ref [33].

A second major issue is anatomical precision. Neuronavigation improves the spatial consistency of stimulation and reduces uncertainty arising from interindividual variability in cortical anatomy ref [36]. MRI-guided placement strategies, although often developed outside stroke populations, illustrate how image-based targeting can optimize coil positioning and thereby enhance the validity of inferences about cortical excitability and network engagement ref [21]. This is especially relevant in lesioned brains, where displacement of landmarks and altered scalp-to-cortex geometry can otherwise confound biomarker interpretation.

When TMS is combined with other modalities, it can move beyond local excitability toward systems-level assessment. Interleaved TMS-fMRI demonstrates that stimulation can produce intensity-dependent bilateral BOLD effects, highlighting the distributed network consequences of focal perturbation and the potential value of combined measures for probing interhemispheric reorganization after stroke ref [14]. Likewise, TMS-EEG can characterize cortical responsiveness directly, but recent work warns that non-transcranial sensory-evoked components remain an inherent source of ambiguity in TMS-evoked potentials ref [34]. Together, these considerations position TMS-based assessment as highly informative for motor recovery studies, provided that navigation, reliability, and artifact control are explicitly addressed.

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) provides a neurophysiological window into post-stroke motor system integrity that complements structural and functional imaging. In clinical investigation, single-pulse and paired-pulse TMS are used to probe corticospinal excitability, motor thresholds, motor evoked potential amplitude, silent period duration, and intracortical inhibition/facilitation, thereby offering mechanistically interpretable markers of residual motor pathway function and cortical reorganization ref [11], ref [39]. In stroke populations, the presence, absence, or gradual re-emergence of motor evoked potentials is particularly informative for tracking corticospinal tract viability and for stratifying patients according to recovery potential ref [39].

The value of TMS increases further when it is integrated with other noninvasive measures. TMS-fMRI links focal perturbation to distributed hemodynamic responses, enabling assessment of how stimulation of spared motor regions engages ipsilesional, contralesional, and subcortical networks, while also highlighting important methodological constraints in causal interpretation and artifact control ref [14]. TMS-EEG extends this logic with millisecond resolution, capturing TMS-evoked cortical responses and connectivity patterns that are not dependent on peripheral output and are therefore useful even when motor evoked potentials are absent or difficult to elicit after severe stroke ref [35].

Taken together, multimodal TMS approaches are well suited for biomarker development in motor rehabilitation. They can characterize both corticospinal output and broader circuit-level responsiveness, helping distinguish compensatory from restorative processes and potentially identify patients most likely to benefit from targeted neuromodulation or task-oriented therapy ref [35], ref [39]. At the same time, careful attention to stimulation parameters, state dependency, and interpretation limits remains essential for reliable use in longitudinal recovery studies ref [11], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) provides a compact neurophysiological framework for probing corticospinal integrity, cortical excitability, and network-level reorganization during post-stroke motor recovery. In neurology, its clinical value lies not only in eliciting motor evoked potentials, but also in quantifying recruitment properties, silent period measures, and interhemispheric interactions that are often altered after stroke, thereby offering biomarkers that complement structural and functional imaging assessments ref [22], ref [23]. More recent conceptual work has further emphasized moving beyond a simple “virtual lesion” interpretation of TMS toward a causal-interrogation tool that can characterize distributed motor networks and state-dependent processing, which is especially relevant when recovery depends on dynamic reweighting across ipsilesional and contralesional regions ref [16].

Evidence from combined fMRI-TMS studies shows that recovery-related changes in motor representation can be tracked across modalities. In patients with rapid motor recovery, convergent shifts in functional activation and TMS-derived motor maps suggest that restoration is associated with reorganization of residual motor cortex rather than a purely compensatory process outside primary motor pathways ref [19]. This multimodal perspective is important in rehabilitation studies because TMS can index whether a treatment is engaging spared corticospinal output pathways, while imaging localizes the broader cortical redistribution that accompanies behavioral gains ref [19], ref [22].

For TMS-based biomarkers to be useful longitudinally, measurement stability is essential. Test-retest work on TMS-EEG evoked potentials indicates that some cortical response components show acceptable reproducibility, supporting their use for repeated monitoring of cortical reactivity and connectivity, although protocol standardization remains critical ref [10]. Likewise, methodological studies indicate that the number of delivered pulses materially affects reliability in neuronavigated TMS outcome measures, underscoring that biomarker sensitivity depends on acquisition design as much as on biological signal ref [29]. Together, these considerations position TMS, TMS-EEG, and neuronavigated mapping as practical tools for stratifying patients and tracking neurophysiological trajectories during post-stroke motor rehabilitation ref [10], ref [23], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Assessment of Motor Recovery - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A clinically oriented assessment framework for post-stroke motor recovery increasingly relies on transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) as a physiological probe of corticospinal tract integrity, cortical excitability, and interhemispheric balance. In this context, measures such as motor evoked potential presence, resting motor threshold, recruitment properties, and paired-pulse indices can complement behavioral scales by identifying residual motor system capacity and stratifying patients according to recovery potential ref [30], ref [33]. These features make TMS particularly valuable when structural damage alone does not fully explain motor impairment.

The interpretability of TMS biomarkers is strengthened when stimulation is anatomically and functionally guided. Neuronavigated TMS improves targeting reproducibility, while evidence for spatial correspondence between TMS hotspots and functional neuroimaging supports the use of multimodal mapping to localize spared motor representations after stroke ref [36]. Such integration is especially relevant in patients with cortical reorganization, where lesion-induced displacement of functional motor areas can reduce the reliability of scalp-based heuristics. A combined imaging-TMS approach therefore helps distinguish true physiological recovery from compensatory recruitment patterns.

Beyond assessment, these biomarkers are directly relevant to treatment selection and monitoring. Reviews of stroke rehabilitation emphasize that baseline excitability asymmetry, corticospinal responsiveness, and the integrity of ipsilesional motor outputs can inform the likely utility of inhibitory versus facilitatory stimulation paradigms and can be tracked longitudinally as markers of intervention responsiveness ref [30], ref [33]. Accordingly, TMS is best viewed not only as a neuromodulation tool, but also as a practical bridge between neuroimaging-defined network status and individualized rehabilitation planning ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is one of the foundational noninvasive brain stimulation modalities in stroke rehabilitation because it can probe and modulate the motor system with relatively high temporal precision. A rapidly changing current in the stimulation coil generates a magnetic field that penetrates the skull and induces an electric field in superficial cortex, thereby depolarizing neuronal elements when sufficient intensity and orientation are achieved ref [41], ref [40]. In the motor system, single-pulse TMS has been especially valuable for assessing corticospinal tract integrity, motor thresholds, motor-evoked potentials, and cortical maps, which together provide a physiological window into post-stroke reorganization ref [15], ref [41].

When delivered repetitively, TMS can produce after-effects that outlast the stimulation period and are commonly interpreted as plasticity-like changes in cortical excitability. Low-frequency stimulation tends to suppress corticospinal excitability, whereas higher-frequency paradigms more often facilitate it, although effects depend on baseline state, lesion characteristics, and network context ref [42], ref [35]. Experimental and conceptual work further suggests that repetitive TMS engages synaptic plasticity mechanisms analogous to long-term potentiation- and long-term depression-like processes, offering a mechanistic rationale for its use in reshaping maladaptive interhemispheric imbalance after stroke ref [37], ref [35].

At the systems level, TMS effects are not restricted to the stimulated gyrus but propagate through distributed motor networks, influencing local excitability, transsynaptic activity, and functional interactions between ipsilesional and contralesional hemispheres ref [40], ref [15]. This network perspective is clinically relevant because motor impairment after stroke reflects disrupted connectivity as much as focal damage. Consistent with this rationale, meta-analytic evidence indicates that repetitive TMS can improve motor outcomes in stroke populations, supporting its role as a therapeutic modality in addition to its established value as a mechanistic and assessment tool ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a principal noninvasive stimulation modality in stroke rehabilitation because its after-effects can be shaped by stimulation frequency and pattern. Low-frequency stimulation is generally used to reduce cortical excitability, whereas higher-frequency protocols are typically intended to facilitate excitability and support motor network recruitment. This bidirectionality has been linked to synaptic plasticity-like processes, including depotentiation- or long-term depression-like effects after slow stimulation, providing a mechanistic basis for suppressing maladaptive hyperexcitability in the contralesional hemisphere after stroke ref [9].

At the physiological level, rTMS influences inhibitory and excitatory intracortical circuits rather than simply changing net output. In healthy subjects, repetitive stimulation alters measures of cortical inhibition, supporting the view that GABAergic mechanisms are central to its effects ref [31]. Animal work further suggests that repeated magnetic stimulation can induce durable changes in neuroplasticity-related markers, although these effects depend strongly on brain state, with different outcomes in awake versus anesthetized preparations ref [12]. These observations are relevant to stroke, where lesion burden, vigilance, task engagement, and concurrent therapy may all modify responsiveness to stimulation.

A related translational issue is how stimulation is delivered. Neuronavigation improves anatomical precision and reproducibility of coil placement, which is especially important in stroke because cortical landmarks may be distorted by lesions and reorganization ref [36]. Beyond TMS, convergent evidence from transcranial direct current stimulation indicates that noninvasive stimulation can modulate cortical GABA levels and resting-state functional connectivity, reinforcing the broader concept that stimulation acts on distributed motor networks rather than isolated cortical sites ref [40]. Consistent with this systems-level view, consensus statements argue that both TMS and tDCS may enhance motor learning and memory formation when appropriately timed with training, thereby offering a mechanistic rationale for pairing stimulation with task-specific rehabilitation ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a central noninvasive stimulation modality in post-stroke motor rehabilitation because it can both probe and modulate corticospinal and cortico-cortical function. Its basic biophysical principle is electromagnetic induction: a rapidly changing current in the coil generates an electric field in superficial cortical tissue, depolarizing neural elements according to coil geometry, field orientation, and membrane properties rather than stimulating cortex uniformly ref [11], ref [31]. Computational work further indicates that TMS effects emerge from interactions between induced fields and local circuit architecture, so stimulation outcome depends not only on delivered intensity but also on the ongoing state of excitatory and inhibitory cortical populations ref [24].

At the physiological level, TMS can induce immediate changes in neuronal firing and longer-lasting shifts in synaptic efficacy that resemble plasticity-like phenomena. In stroke, these properties support two complementary strategies: facilitating residual activity in the ipsilesional motor cortex or suppressing maladaptive overactivity in the contralesional hemisphere to rebalance interhemispheric interactions within motor networks ref [39]. Repetitive protocols are therefore interpreted not simply as focal excitation or inhibition, but as interventions capable of reshaping distributed motor circuitry, including corticospinal output, intracortical inhibition, and network-level connectivity relevant for recovery ref [11], ref [24], ref [39].

Mechanistic characterization has been strengthened by multimodal approaches. TMS-EEG can capture stimulation-evoked cortical responses and effective connectivity beyond the motor system, offering a direct window into how stroke alters reactivity and propagation within damaged networks ref [35]. At the same time, emerging ultrasound-based neuromodulation provides a useful point of comparison: transcranial focused and unfocused ultrasound rely on acoustic rather than electromagnetic energy and may offer different trade-offs in spatial precision and depth of penetration, although their role in motor stroke rehabilitation remains less established than that of TMS ref [37]. Together, these modalities frame rehabilitation neuromodulation as targeted manipulation of excitability, connectivity, and plasticity rather than simple regional activation.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a central neuromodulatory modality in stroke rehabilitation because patterned pulse trains can induce lasting changes in cortical excitability beyond the stimulation period. Classical rTMS formulations exploit frequency-dependent effects, with low-frequency stimulation generally suppressing excitability and higher-frequency stimulation tending to facilitate it, thereby providing a practical framework for rebalancing activity across damaged motor networks after stroke ref [42], ref [23], ref [22].

The mechanistic rationale in post-stroke motor recovery is closely tied to interhemispheric competition models. Following unilateral stroke, excessive inhibitory influence from the contralesional hemisphere may further depress ipsilesional motor cortex output; accordingly, inhibitory rTMS over the unaffected hemisphere, excitatory stimulation over the affected hemisphere, or dual-hemisphere approaches have been used to normalize transcallosal interactions and promote functional reorganization ref [31], ref [19], ref [42]. Although dual-hemisphere protocols were first explored extensively in domains such as aphasia, they are mechanistically relevant to motor rehabilitation because they operationalize simultaneous downregulation of maladaptive contralesional activity and upregulation of residual ipsilesional capacity ref [31].

At the systems level, these effects are not limited to hand motor cortex. Stroke studies and reviews suggest that rTMS can reshape distributed motor representations and influence gait, balance, and lower-limb control, indicating network-level modulation of corticospinal and supraspinal circuits rather than purely focal excitation changes ref [38], ref [19]. Thus, rTMS in stroke rehabilitation is best understood as a plasticity-oriented intervention that targets excitability, interhemispheric coupling, and functional motor network reorganization in a protocol-dependent manner ref [23], ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities and Mechanisms in Stroke Rehabilitation - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Beyond conventional cortical M1 protocols, emerging noninvasive stimulation approaches are expanding the mechanistic scope of post-stroke rehabilitation. Reviews of transcranial magnetic stimulation emphasize that stimulation effects are not limited to local excitability shifts, but can engage distributed motor networks, alter interregional synchronization, and potentially reshape maladaptive hemispheric interactions that follow stroke ref [48], ref [12]. In this broader framework, stimulation target selection has increasingly moved from a purely cortical-lesion model toward network-oriented modulation.

Evidence for such network-level action is illustrated by studies showing that excitatory and inhibitory repetitive TMS can induce bidirectional changes in interhemispheric resting-state functional connectivity, supporting the idea that stimulation can rebalance communication between damaged and contralesional motor systems ref [11]. Cerebellar stimulation further extends this logic: noninvasive magnetic stimulation of the cerebellum has been shown to facilitate cortico-bulbar projections, highlighting the capacity of extra-cortical targets to influence motor output pathways and suggesting a role for cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits in functional recovery ref [31]. Mechanistically, these effects are consistent with cellular models in which repetitive magnetic stimulation alters synaptic efficacy, calcium-dependent signaling, gene expression, and inhibitory-excitatory balance, thereby supporting longer-lasting plastic reorganization rather than transient excitation alone ref [34].

Other waveform strategies may also prove relevant to stroke rehabilitation. Short-duration transcranial random noise stimulation has been reported to modulate cortical excitability, implying that stochastic electrical stimulation may enhance neural responsiveness through mechanisms distinct from polarity-dependent stimulation paradigms ref [16]. Although clinical translation remains incomplete, recent stroke-focused reviews argue that the field is moving toward more individualized protocols integrating target choice, stimulation polarity/frequency, and timing with behavioral therapy, while also noting that routine clinical adoption still requires stronger evidence and protocol standardization ref [30], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is one of the most studied noninvasive stimulation approaches for post-stroke motor rehabilitation, particularly for upper-limb paresis. Its therapeutic rationale derives from frequency-dependent modulation of corticospinal excitability: low-frequency stimulation generally suppresses excitability, whereas higher-frequency stimulation tends to facilitate it, providing a mechanistic basis for either downregulating the contralesional hemisphere or upregulating ipsilesional motor cortex after stroke ref [5], ref [12]. These protocol options are also grounded in broader evidence that TMS can probe and reshape cortical motor-control networks relevant to motor recovery ref [15], ref [35].

In clinical application, most rTMS protocols target primary motor cortex and are selected according to the patient’s residual corticospinal integrity, lesion burden, and presumed interhemispheric imbalance. Imaging-informed work has shown that TMS influences not only local cortex but distributed cortical and subcortical motor circuits, supporting the view that behavioral gains may reflect network-level reorganization rather than isolated focal effects ref [25], ref [31]. This has encouraged increasing use of navigated TMS to improve targeting precision and reproducibility, especially when post-stroke anatomy is distorted and conventional scalp-based localization may be unreliable ref [26].

At the evidence-synthesis level, meta-analytic findings indicate that rTMS can produce modest but significant improvements in motor function after stroke, although effect sizes vary across stimulation frequency, hemisphere targeted, recovery stage, and concomitant rehabilitation intensity ref [39]. Overall, the literature supports rTMS as an adjunct rather than a standalone therapy, with the strongest case emerging when stimulation is embedded within task-specific motor training and guided by individualized neurophysiological or imaging markers ref [12], ref [31], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
For upper-limb retraining after stroke, a central therapeutic rationale for noninvasive brain stimulation is to prime practice-dependent plasticity rather than to act as a stand-alone intervention. Consensus work indicates that both transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can influence motor learning and memory formation, supporting their use as adjuncts to repetitive task practice, constraint-based training, or robot-assisted therapy when the goal is to strengthen retention of newly acquired movements rather than only produce transient performance gains ref [15].

Protocol selection in this context is often framed around restoring a more favorable excitatory-inhibitory balance within the motor network. tDCS studies show that stimulation can modulate local GABAergic tone and resting-state functional connectivity, suggesting a mechanistic basis for pairing anodal ipsilesional stimulation with skill training in patients with reduced corticospinal output, or for using inhibitory approaches when maladaptive network dominance is suspected ref [40]. These network-level effects are especially relevant for proximal arm and hand recovery, where gains depend on coordinated recruitment across distributed sensorimotor regions rather than isolated cortical excitation alone ref [40].

Clinically, these observations support a stratified application strategy: in early rehabilitation, stimulation may be used to enhance encoding of emerging motor patterns, whereas in later phases it may be better leveraged to improve consolidation, reduce learned nonuse, and increase responsiveness to intensive practice ref [15]. Although effect sizes remain heterogeneous across trials, the available evidence justifies integrating stimulation parameters with symptom profile, training dose, and recovery stage, particularly for patients whose upper-limb progress plateaus under conventional therapy alone ref [15], ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A major therapeutic use of noninvasive brain stimulation in post-stroke motor rehabilitation is the treatment of lower-limb impairment, gait dysfunction, and balance deficits. In this domain, protocol selection has generally followed the same physiological logic used for upper-limb recovery: facilitating residual activity in the ipsilesional motor network or suppressing maladaptive interhemispheric inhibition from the contralesional hemisphere. Reviews focused on stroke rehabilitation indicate that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and related stimulation approaches can improve lower-extremity motor performance, although effect sizes are typically more modest and heterogeneous than for hand function because gait depends on distributed bilateral and subcortical circuits rather than a single focal cortical representation [25], [16].

This therapeutic heterogeneity is especially important when choosing stimulation targets. The leg area of primary motor cortex is anatomically deeper and closer to the interhemispheric fissure, which makes dose delivery, coil orientation, and reproducible targeting more challenging than for hand muscles [13], [15], [24]. Methodological work on navigation and scalp-to-cortex variability further suggests that individualized targeting may be particularly relevant for lower-limb protocols, where small errors in position or field strength can alter engagement of corticospinal outputs [11], [43]. Accordingly, clinical application for gait and balance often benefits from neuronavigation, careful motor-threshold adjustment, and pairing stimulation with task-specific walking or balance training rather than using stimulation as a stand-alone intervention [16], [42].

From a recovery-phase perspective, the most plausible use case is as an adjunct during active rehabilitation, when stimulation can bias plasticity in locomotor networks and potentially enhance training responsiveness. TMS-based studies of stroke recovery support this biomarker-guided approach by showing that corticospinal excitability, interhemispheric balance, and residual motor map organization can help identify patients with sufficient substrate for response and can inform whether facilitatory, inhibitory, or bilateral paradigms are preferable [39], [16]. Thus, for lower-limb and balance rehabilitation, the current evidence favors individualized, physiology-informed stimulation embedded within multimodal therapy rather than a uniform protocol applied across all stroke phenotypes [25], [39].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A major therapeutic application of noninvasive brain stimulation in stroke concerns lower-limb recovery, especially gait and balance. In this domain, protocols have generally adapted the same interhemispheric rebalancing logic used for the upper limb, but with greater attention to bilateral network organization and the involvement of supplementary motor, premotor, and leg-area motor representations. Reviews of the field indicate that both repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and related noninvasive stimulation approaches can improve walking performance, postural control, and lower-extremity motor scores, although effect sizes vary with chronicity, lesion profile, and the concomitant intensity of task-specific rehabilitation ref [38], ref [42].

From a protocol standpoint, inhibitory low-frequency stimulation of the contralesional hemisphere and excitatory high-frequency stimulation of the ipsilesional motor system remain the dominant strategies, but lower-limb outcomes appear especially sensitive to state dependence and network context. Foundational mechanistic accounts of TMS emphasize that stimulation effects are not uniform; they depend on baseline excitability, coil position, stimulation frequency, and ongoing sensorimotor activity, all of which are highly relevant when targeting locomotor circuits engaged during stepping and balance training ref [23], ref [22], ref [42]. This helps explain why studies pairing stimulation with physiotherapy, treadmill training, or balance exercises often report more consistent gains than stimulation delivered in isolation ref [38].

Neurophysiological and imaging observations further support this rehabilitation model. Early recovery studies showed that changes in motor representation can accompany rapid post-stroke improvement, suggesting that stimulation may be most effective when it amplifies an already evolving reorganization process rather than attempting to impose plasticity on a static network ref [19]. Accordingly, in subacute patients with residual descending pathway integrity, facilitatory stimulation of the affected hemisphere may reinforce adaptive re-engagement of motor output, whereas in more chronic or asymmetrical cases, suppressing maladaptive contralesional influence may be preferable. Overall, current evidence supports brain stimulation as an adjunct—not a standalone therapy—for gait and balance rehabilitation, with individualized targeting and timing remaining central to clinical benefit ref [38], ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Applications of Brain Stimulation for Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Beyond limb motor recovery, noninvasive stimulation has also been explored for bulbar motor dysfunction, particularly post-stroke dysphagia, which is highly relevant to functional rehabilitation and overall disability. A systematic review and meta-analysis indicates that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can improve swallowing outcomes after stroke, supporting dysphagia as a clinically meaningful extension of motor rehabilitation rather than a separate domain ref [37]. This literature also suggests that protocol selection matters, with benefit influenced by stimulation frequency, lesion hemisphere, and the cortical representation targeted within the swallowing network ref [37].

From a therapeutic standpoint, these findings align with broader stroke-rehabilitation frameworks proposing that noninvasive brain stimulation is most effective when matched to the underlying imbalance in cortical excitability and paired with task-specific training ref [33]. Reviews of clinical application emphasize that inhibitory stimulation of the contralesional hemisphere, excitatory stimulation of the ipsilesional hemisphere, and in some cases bilateral strategies have all been tested in stroke, but translation into routine care remains limited by heterogeneity in patients, outcome measures, and stimulation dosing ref [30], ref [33]. In dysphagia, this heterogeneity is especially important because bilateral corticobulbar control may make simple interhemispheric models less sufficient than in hand-motor recovery ref [37].

Taken together, the available evidence suggests that brain stimulation has therapeutic promise across a broader motor phenotype that includes swallowing, but also illustrates the field’s central challenge: effects are plausible and often positive at the group level, yet protocol standardization and patient stratification remain inadequate for widespread clinical adoption ref [30], ref [33], ref [37]. Future rehabilitation trials should therefore compare lesion-informed targeting and phase-specific dosing across both appendicular and bulbar motor deficits to determine where stimulation adds value beyond conventional therapy alone ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central pillar of precision post-stroke neuromodulation is imaging-guided target localization. Neuronavigated TMS improves anatomical accuracy relative to conventional scalp-based heuristics and enables stimulation to be aligned with each patient’s lesion anatomy and preserved cortical landmarks, which is particularly important when infarcts distort standard motor maps ref [26]. Therapy studies have also shown that “standard” coil positioning can be unreliable when checked against neuronavigation, underscoring why individualized targeting is critical for reproducible dosing and interpretation of treatment effects ref [28].

Personalization also depends on adapting stimulation intensity to individual anatomy. Because scalp-cortex distance influences the effective electric field at the cortical surface, simple distance-based scaling metrics offer a practical way to normalize motor threshold estimates across patients with differing atrophy, edema resolution, or post-stroke structural asymmetry ref [32]. More broadly, consensus work on combining transcranial stimulation with neuroimaging argues that structural and functional imaging should be integrated not only for target selection, but also for stratifying candidates and monitoring network-level responses to intervention ref [31].

Although most evidence has focused on motor recovery, multimodal studies illustrate the broader rehabilitation logic of biomarker-guided stimulation. For example, combined rTMS-PET work in post-stroke aphasia linked stimulation effects to metabolically defined reorganization in the contralesional inferior frontal gyrus, demonstrating how imaging can identify compensatory versus maladaptive recruitment patterns ref [42]. In the motor domain, meta-analytic evidence supports beneficial effects of rTMS on post-stroke motor function, but also highlights substantial heterogeneity, reinforcing the need for image- and physiology-informed protocols rather than one-size-fits-all stimulation paradigms ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central precision-rehabilitation strategy is to use structural and functional imaging to personalize where stimulation is delivered, rather than relying on scalp heuristics. MRI-guided neuronavigation improves spatial correspondence between intended cortical targets and coil position, and work on image-based targeting has shown that individualized anatomy can substantially refine stimulation placement relative to conventional rules of thumb ref [54], ref [21], ref [36]. Although much of this literature originates outside stroke, the principle is directly transferable to post-stroke motor rehabilitation, where lesion-induced distortion of anatomy and network reorganization make standard positioning particularly unreliable.

Functional imaging can further personalize target selection by identifying task-relevant or network-relevant cortical sites. fMRI-guided TMS studies demonstrate that stimulation can be directed to functionally localized regions rather than only anatomically defined landmarks, supporting a biomarker-driven approach to selecting ipsilesional, contralesional, or secondary motor-network targets in stroke ref [20], ref [36]. Concurrent or interleaved TMS-fMRI also shows that stimulation effects propagate beyond the local site in an intensity-dependent and bilateral manner, underscoring that dosing and target choice should be informed by network-level responses rather than by focal anatomy alone ref [14].

These imaging-guided concepts align naturally with combination rehabilitation paradigms. Consensus work on noninvasive stimulation and motor learning argues that stimulation is most likely to be beneficial when paired with training that engages the targeted circuit, while neurochemical-imaging studies suggest that stimulation-induced changes in inhibition and resting-state connectivity may provide mechanistic biomarkers for identifying responders and optimizing treatment timing ref [15], ref [40]. Together, these findings support a personalized framework in which imaging informs target localization, stimulation intensity, and integration with task practice or technology-assisted motor training.

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central direction in precision post-stroke rehabilitation is the use of circuit-level biomarkers to personalize when, where, and with what behavioral context stimulation should be delivered. Multimodal methods such as TMS-EEG and TMS combined with functional imaging provide complementary information on cortical reactivity, effective connectivity, and network recruitment, offering a more individualized basis for selecting stimulation targets than anatomy alone ref [14], ref [35]. In stroke, this strategy is especially relevant because residual motor function depends on heterogeneous patterns of ipsilesional preservation, contralesional compensation, and interhemispheric imbalance, all of which can be probed with TMS-based physiological measures ref [39].

Resting-state connectivity findings further support biomarker-guided treatment selection. A systematic review of rTMS effects on resting-state networks indicates that stimulation can reshape distributed connectivity rather than only local excitability, suggesting that baseline network organization and treatment-induced network shifts may serve as useful markers for stratifying patients and monitoring response ref [9]. Although much of this literature is not stroke-specific, the implication for motor rehabilitation is clear: patients with different connectivity phenotypes may require different stimulation polarities, hemispheric targets, or pairing with task practice to drive adaptive reorganization ref [9], ref [39].

Combination paradigms are therefore gaining prominence. Broader work on pairing noninvasive stimulation with behavioral interventions shows that stimulation is often most effective when embedded within active training contexts, rather than delivered as an isolated neuromodulatory add-on ref [23]. Stroke studies outside the motor domain also reinforce this principle: in post-stroke aphasia, rTMS combined with language-oriented rehabilitation and network-informed targeting has produced measurable behavioral gains in pilot randomized work, illustrating how stimulation can be integrated with domain-specific therapy to exploit residual plasticity ref [56]. For motor recovery, these observations support multimodal programs in which imaging and neurophysiology are used not only to localize targets, but also to determine the optimal coupling of stimulation with practice, robotics, or BCI-driven feedback ref [14], ref [35], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A major direction in precision rehabilitation is the coupling of noninvasive stimulation with function-specific training rather than delivering stimulation as an isolated intervention. Early combined fMRI–TMS work showed that rapid motor recovery after stroke is accompanied by evolving shifts in motor representation across cortical regions, supporting the idea that stimulation should be aligned with the current organization of the recovering network rather than a fixed anatomical target ref [19]. This logic motivates biomarker-informed pairing of stimulation with concurrent motor practice, where imaging and neurophysiology can help identify whether ipsilesional facilitation, contralesional suppression, or bilateral modulation is most appropriate.

Combination strategies are also relevant beyond upper-limb motor recovery. Reviews of noninvasive brain stimulation for gait, balance, and lower-limb dysfunction indicate that stimulation tends to be most meaningful when embedded in task-oriented rehabilitation, such as gait training or balance exercises, because these paradigms may better translate transient excitability changes into durable functional gains ref [38]. In this context, imaging-guided personalization can be used to select cortical or cerebellar targets linked to locomotor control and to adapt dosing according to residual network integrity, lesion distribution, and the specific motor domain being trained ref [19], ref [38].

Although much of the personalization literature in stroke focuses on motor deficits, aphasia studies offer an instructive model for multimodal and bilateral designs. Dual-hemisphere repetitive TMS protocols for poststroke aphasia explicitly combine facilitation of damaged-language networks with suppression of maladaptive contralesional activity, illustrating how network-informed stimulation can be integrated with behavioral therapy in a domain-specific manner ref [31]. Conceptually, the same principle is highly relevant to motor rehabilitation: imaging and physiological markers can guide whether bilateral, unilateral, or sequential stimulation should accompany robotic practice, repetitive task training, or BCI-assisted therapy, with the goal of matching intervention architecture to each patient’s residual network state ref [19], ref [31], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Imaging-Guided Personalization and Combination Rehabilitation Strategies - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A practical implication of precision rehabilitation is that stimulation should not be viewed as a stand-alone intervention, but as a modulator of network state that can be paired with behaviorally relevant therapy. Reviews of post-stroke rTMS and tDCS emphasize that clinical benefit is most likely when stimulation parameters, hemispheric target, and timing are matched to the patient’s impairment profile and integrated with active motor practice rather than delivered in isolation ref [30], ref [33]. In this framework, imaging and neurophysiological markers are useful not only for patient selection, but also for deciding whether to upregulate ipsilesional regions, suppress maladaptive contralesional activity, or adopt bilateral strategies.

Imaging-guided targeting further strengthens combination approaches by improving anatomical and functional specificity. The reported spatial congruence between neuronavigated TMS targets and functional neuroimaging supports the use of individualized MRI/fMRI information to align stimulation with residual motor networks ref [36]. At the systems level, rTMS can induce direction-specific changes in interhemispheric resting-state connectivity, indicating that excitatory and inhibitory protocols reshape distributed network interactions differently ref [11]. Such findings provide a mechanistic rationale for coupling stimulation with task-oriented training, robotic practice, or brain-computer interface paradigms that exploit transient windows of heightened plasticity after network rebalancing.

The value of personalized multimodal rehabilitation is also evident beyond limb motor recovery. In post-stroke dysphagia, systematic evidence suggests that rTMS can serve as an adjunctive therapy, supporting the broader principle that stimulation effects may be amplified when paired with domain-specific rehabilitation targeting the affected sensorimotor system ref [37]. Overall, current syntheses suggest that the next step for clinical translation is not simply to ask whether stimulation works, but for whom, where, and in combination with which training context it works best ref [30], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central methodological barrier in post-stroke neuromodulation is the large interindividual variability in physiological and behavioral response. Even when nominal stimulation parameters are held constant, rTMS effects on cortical excitability can differ markedly across participants, complicating dose selection, responder identification, and cross-trial comparison ref [10]. This variability is amplified in stroke by lesion heterogeneity, altered network organization, and fluctuating excitability states, making simple protocol transfer from healthy cohorts unreliable. More broadly, noninvasive stimulation-induced plasticity is highly dependent on baseline physiology and prior activity, so observed treatment effects may reflect context-sensitive metaplasticity rather than a fixed protocol effect ref [35].

A related challenge is state dependency: the effect of stimulation depends on the functional condition of the targeted network at the moment of delivery ref [18]. In rehabilitation studies, differences in task engagement, fatigue, medication status, and timing relative to motor training can therefore produce divergent outcomes despite apparently similar designs. These issues are compounded by imprecise targeting. Standard scalp-based coil placement shows limited reliability when checked against neuronavigation, raising concern that negative or inconsistent findings may partly reflect spatial error rather than biological inefficacy ref [28]. Navigated TMS improves anatomical precision and supports more reproducible targeting, particularly in patients with distorted post-stroke anatomy ref [26].

Future trials should therefore move toward individualized dosing and multimodal, physiology-informed targeting. Adjusting stimulation intensity for scalp-cortex distance can reduce one source of between-subject variance in effective cortical dose ref [32], while combined stimulation-neuroimaging frameworks can better characterize target engagement and network-level effects ref [31]. Methodological rigor must be paired with standardized safety procedures and ethical oversight, especially when enrolling medically complex stroke populations or testing intensified protocols ref [58]. Together, these steps are essential for improving reproducibility and translating noninvasive imaging-stimulation paradigms into dependable rehabilitation tools.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A persistent methodological barrier in post-stroke stimulation trials is the difficulty of constructing valid control conditions and artifact-free readouts. So-called sham TMS is not always physiologically inert; some sham configurations can generate sensory and even cortical effects that narrow the contrast between active and control arms and complicate efficacy estimates ref [9]. The problem is amplified in TMS-EEG studies, where the recorded TMS-evoked response may contain substantial non-transcranial components arising from auditory, somatosensory, and peripheral co-stimulation, creating ambiguity in the interpretation of cortical biomarkers ref [37].

Reproducibility is further limited by variability in targeting and in basic motor physiology measures. International consensus work has emphasized that TMS studies should report key methodological details systematically, including coil orientation, intensity selection, muscle pre-activation, and outcome definitions, to improve interpretability and cross-study comparability ref [22]. Even under controlled conditions, reliability differs across muscle representations, indicating that corticospinal metrics used to stratify or monitor stroke recovery are not equally stable across targets ref [33]. These issues are especially relevant in heterogeneous stroke populations, where lesion location, corticospinal tract integrity, and compensatory recruitment already increase measurement variance.

Future trials should therefore move toward standardized, image-informed stimulation workflows and explicit safety monitoring. MRI-guided neuronavigation can improve coil placement precision and reduce spatial uncertainty relative to heuristic positioning, supporting better target engagement and multicenter harmonization ref [21], ref [36]. At the same time, accelerated protocols such as theta-burst stimulation appear broadly safe when delivered within recommended parameters, but systematic review data still support careful screening and adverse-event reporting, particularly in medically complex rehabilitation cohorts ref [16]. Together, rigorous sham design, artifact-aware neurophysiology, standardized reporting, and navigated targeting are central to translational progress.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A persistent translational challenge is the construction of credible control conditions and the management of expectancy effects in stimulation trials. Work on therapeutic TMS has shown that perceived treatment assignment and participant expectation can materially influence reported outcomes, underscoring that placebo responses are not peripheral but integral to trial interpretation ref [13]. This issue is especially relevant in post-stroke rehabilitation, where intensive therapist contact and high patient motivation may amplify nonspecific effects. Methodological guidance from stimulation research further indicates that sham design, sensory matching, and transparent reporting of blinding procedures are essential for valid between-group comparisons ref [30], ref [11].

A second barrier concerns mechanistic uncertainty: identical nominal stimulation protocols may engage different neural populations depending on lesion anatomy, cortical state, and network reorganization after stroke. Computational accounts emphasize that TMS effects emerge from interactions between induced electric fields and local circuit properties rather than from stimulation frequency alone ref [24]. Multimodal approaches can reduce this ambiguity. TMS-EEG offers direct access to cortical reactivity and connectivity, while concurrent or interleaved imaging helps map distributed network consequences, although both approaches introduce technical and interpretive limitations that must be carefully managed ref [35], ref [14].

Future studies should therefore move beyond one-size-fits-all protocols toward biomarker-informed designs. In stroke specifically, TMS can stratify corticospinal integrity, interhemispheric imbalance, and residual plastic potential, making it useful not only as an intervention but also as a tool for patient selection and response monitoring ref [39]. More rigorous protocol standardization, mechanistic modeling, and multimodal validation should improve reproducibility and help identify which patients are most likely to benefit from individualized noninvasive stimulation strategies ref [11], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A persistent translational barrier is measurement reliability. In stroke studies, treatment effects are often inferred from changes in motor-evoked potentials, cortical maps, or TMS-EEG responses, yet these indices can show substantial within-subject and between-session variability. Recent work suggests that reliability can be improved by optimizing sampling density, as the number of delivered pulses materially affects the stability of neuronavigated TMS outcome measures, while TMS-EEG evoked potentials also demonstrate only component-specific test-retest robustness ref [29], ref [10]. This implies that underpowered acquisition protocols may obscure true rehabilitation-related neurophysiological change.

A second challenge concerns standardization across devices, targets, and species. Foundational reviews of TMS emphasize that stimulation effects depend strongly on coil geometry, pulse waveform, intensity selection, and ongoing brain state, complicating direct comparison across trials ref [23], ref [42], ref [22]. Comparative electric-field modeling further shows that the spatial distribution and strength of induced fields differ markedly across mouse, monkey, and human brains, underscoring why mechanistic insights from preclinical models cannot be transferred uncritically to clinical stroke protocols ref [17]. In rehabilitation studies, this problem is amplified for lower-limb and gait interventions, where heterogeneous cortical targets and outcome measures continue to limit synthesis across studies ref [38].

Future work should therefore prioritize harmonized acquisition and reporting standards, including neuronavigated targeting, explicit pulse-count justifications, reliability-aware endpoint selection, and routine field modeling when possible. Safety data remain broadly reassuring for noninvasive stimulation, with very large prospective datasets indicating favorable tolerability when established protocols are followed, although vulnerable populations still require dedicated monitoring and dose calibration ref [38]. For post-stroke motor rehabilitation, the key next step is not simply more trials, but better-calibrated, reproducible, and safety-conscious trials that can support clinically actionable biomarkers and stimulation prescriptions.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Challenges, Safety, and Future Directions - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Future translation will depend on moving from proof-of-concept stimulation studies to standardized, precision-oriented rehabilitation workflows. A persistent barrier is the mismatch between nominal scalp targets and the true cortical regions engaged, which can be reduced through neuronavigation and integration with functional imaging, thereby improving anatomical and functional specificity in post-stroke interventions [ref 36]. At the same time, the growing interest in deeper or broader-field stimulation highlights the need for individualized electric-field modeling, because coil geometry and head anatomy strongly influence the depth–focality trade-off and may alter both efficacy and off-target effects [ref 13].

Another priority is harmonization of trial methodology. Reviews of therapeutic TMS across neurological disorders and stroke specifically emphasize that variation in patient selection, lesion site, chronicity, stimulation dose, outcome timing, and concomitant therapy continues to limit reproducibility and clinical readiness [ref 4, ref 30, ref 33]. Progress will therefore require multicenter protocols with explicit reporting of targeting strategy, motor threshold determination, session spacing, and rehabilitation co-interventions, as well as biomarker-guided stratification rather than one-size-fits-all stimulation paradigms [ref 12, ref 30].

Safety remains favorable overall, but implementation in rehabilitation should be accompanied by structured surveillance and population-specific precautions. Foundational TMS overviews and disease-focused reviews indicate that adverse events are usually mild when established parameters are respected, yet seizure risk, discomfort, and hearing-related issues still require protocol discipline [ref 12, ref 4]. Although pediatric data cannot be directly extrapolated to stroke, systematic safety evidence in younger populations illustrates the value of rigorous monitoring frameworks, conservative dosing, and transparent adverse-event reporting for vulnerable groups and emerging protocols [ref 17].
